blocks.text: Security testing systematically verifies that the defensive layers covered earlier in this module, sanitization, validation, filtering, guardrails, actually work as intended, using a repeatable, automated test suite built from known attack categories rather than occasional, informal manual checks.

This topic covers building a test suite from known attack categories, automating security tests as regression checks, testing each defense layer individually and the whole system together, and how systematic security testing differs from the more creative, exploratory red teaming covered in the next topic.
1. What Security Testing Means Here

blocks.alt: Building on prompt guardrails, security testing provides systematic, repeatable verification

blocks.text: Security testing in this context means running a defined, repeatable set of test cases against a system, specifically designed to check whether known categories of attack, injection, jailbreak, data leakage, are actually being caught by the defenses currently in place.
2. Building a Test Suite From Known Attack Categories

blocks.alt: Injection test cases, jailbreak test cases, and data leakage test cases get built into one suite

blocks.text: This connects directly to every earlier topic in this module, a well built security test suite includes concrete test cases representing each known category, an injection attempt embedded in retrieved content, a jailbreak attempt using roleplay framing, a scenario designed to check for sensitive data leakage.
3. Manual Checks vs an Automated Regression Suite

blocks.alt: A manual, one-off check is compared against an automated regression test suite

blocks.text: This connects directly to the automated regression testing practice covered in the earlier Prompt Debugging topic, a manual, one-time security check catches problems only at the moment it happens to be run, an automated suite run consistently, ideally on every meaningful change, catches a regression the moment it gets introduced.
4. Testing Each Defense Layer Individually

blocks.alt: Sanitization, validation, and filtering each get tested alone

blocks.text: This connects directly to sanitization, input validation, and output filtering, each covered earlier in this module, testing each layer individually, does sanitization actually neutralize the specific delimiter breaking sequence it targets, does validation actually reject the oversized input it should, isolates exactly which layer is working and which one needs attention.

blocks.text: 5. Testing the Complete System Together

blocks.alt: All layers combined get tested as one complete system

blocks.text: This connects directly to the system prompt evaluation checklist covered in an earlier module, individual layers passing their own tests does not guarantee the complete system, sanitization, validation, guardrails, and the main model together, actually stops a genuine end-to-end attack attempt, whole-system testing catches interaction effects individual layer tests would miss.

blocks.title: This mirrors the same insight from system prompt evaluation
blocks.content: Just as testing persona, role, and safety instructions individually is not enough to catch how they interact, testing each security layer alone is not enough to guarantee the complete defense pipeline actually holds up together.

blocks.text: 6. Security Testing vs Red Teaming

blocks.alt: Security testing covers systematic, known categories, red teaming covers creative, adversarial exploration

blocks.text: Security testing, covered in this topic, runs a defined, repeatable suite against known attack categories, red teaming, covered in the next topic, is a more creative, exploratory process specifically aimed at discovering genuinely novel attack angles a predefined test suite would not have anticipated, the two practices are complementary.
7. Tracking Security Test Results Over Time

blocks.alt: Test results tracked over time catch regressions early

blocks.text: This connects directly to prompt versioning, covered in an earlier module, tracking security test pass rates across versions reveals whether a change to the prompt, model, or guardrail configuration accidentally weakened a previously working defense, catching a security regression before it reaches production.
8. A Worked Security Test Suite Example

A team building a document processing assistant maintains a security test suite with fifteen injection test cases, ten jailbreak test cases, and eight data leakage test cases, run automatically on every change to the prompt or guardrail configuration, catching a specific regression when an unrelated prompt change accidentally weakened their delimiter handling for one injection test case.
9. Security Testing as an Ongoing Practice

This connects directly to the arms race concept covered in the earlier Jailbreak Attacks topic, a security test suite needs to grow over time as new attack categories become known, treating it as a living, continuously expanding asset rather than a fixed set written once and never revisited.
Worked Example

A team relying only on occasional manual security spot checks discovers, after an unrelated prompt update, that their previously working jailbreak defense had quietly stopped working for one specific framing category, the change had been live for two weeks before anyone happened to notice during a manual check.

Building an automated security test suite covering this and other known categories, run on every change going forward, would have caught this exact regression within minutes of the change being made rather than two weeks later, prompting the team to invest in exactly this kind of systematic, repeatable testing.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying on occasional manual security checks instead of an automated, repeatable test suite
Testing individual defense layers but never testing the complete system together end to end
Letting a security test suite go stale, never expanding it as new attack categories become known
Confusing systematic security testing with the more creative, exploratory red teaming process, covered in the next topic

blocks.text: Practice

Build a small security test suite for a system you have designed or could design, including at least two injection test cases, two jailbreak test cases, and one data leakage test case, and define what a passing result actually means for each one.
Key Takeaway

Security testing systematically verifies defensive layers using a repeatable test suite built from known attack categories, testing individual layers and the complete system together, automated and tracked over time to catch regressions early, complementary to but distinct from the more creative, exploratory red teaming process covered in the next topic.
